lede: Your body fights microorganisms in three ways: it keeps them out, it engulfs the ones that get in, and it makes antibodies that fit one kind exactly. It also remembers, which is why the same illness rarely strikes twice. Nearly every mark here is a precise word.
can: Name the barriers and describe how blood clots at a cut.
Explain how antibodies fit antigens, clump microorganisms, and how phagocytes finish the job.
Explain the faster second response with memory lymphocytes, and tell active from passive immunity.

caption: Three lines of defence: keep microorganisms out, engulf the ones that get in, and target one kind with antibodies.

md: The first line of defence stops microorganisms getting in at all. The **skin** is a **barrier** they cannot cross. **Mucous membranes** line the nose and airways: their sticky mucus **traps** microorganisms, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it to the throat to be swallowed.

caption: A clot seals a cut: fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells, and a scab forms on top.

md: A cut opens a gap, so **blood clotting** closes it. The plasma carries a protein, **fibrinogen**, dissolved in it. At a cut, **platelets** set off its change into **fibrin**, which is not soluble: long threads that tangle into a mesh.

stem: A cook cuts a finger while chopping onions. Describe how a clot forms at the cut. [3]

steps.working: Platelets at the cut cause soluble fibrinogen in the plasma to change into insoluble fibrin.
steps.decision: Start at the cut with the platelets: they begin the change, and the protein's two names are the first mark.

steps.working: The fibrin threads form a mesh that traps red blood cells, making a clot.
steps.decision: Say what the threads do: a mesh that catches cells is the clot itself.

steps.working: The clot dries into a scab, which stops blood loss and keeps microorganisms out.
steps.decision: Finish with what the clot is for: both jobs, blood in and microorganisms out.

prompt: A medicine stops fibrinogen from changing into fibrin. What happens when someone taking it cuts a finger?
options: the blood does not clot, so the bleeding goes on longer
the cut clots faster than usual
no white blood cells reach the cut
answer: the blood does not clot, so the bleeding goes on longer
explain: Steps 1 and 2 of the See it: fibrinogen must become fibrin, whose threads make the mesh that traps blood cells. Stop that change and no mesh forms, so no clot: the bleeding goes on longer.

optionNotes.option: the cut clots faster than usual
optionNotes.why: Without fibrin there are no threads to make a mesh, so a clot cannot form at all, let alone faster.

optionNotes.option: no white blood cells reach the cut
optionNotes.why: The medicine does not touch white blood cells; what fails is the fibrin mesh that makes the clot.

twin.prompt: A person's plasma has almost no fibrinogen. What happens at a cut?
options: no fibrin mesh forms, so the blood does not clot
the skin grows over the cut at once
twin.answer: no fibrin mesh forms, so the blood does not clot
twin.explain: Fibrin is made from fibrinogen; with almost none there is nothing to make the threads, so no mesh and no clot. Platelets make no antibodies.

caption: The antibody's tip is the reverse of the antigen's shape, so the two fit together.

md: A microorganism that gets past the barriers carries molecules on its surface called **antigens**, and each kind has its own shape. White blood cells called **lymphocytes** respond by making **antibodies** whose shape is **complementary** to that antigen: the reverse of it, so the two fit like a key in its lock.

title: Why one antibody fits one microorganism
md: A complementary shape fits one antigen only, so a new microorganism needs new antibodies, and making them takes several days. The shapes are never the same: a copy of the antigen's shape could not fit over it.

stem: A child's lymphocytes have made antibodies against the measles virus. Explain why these antibodies do not attach to a chickenpox virus. [2]

steps.working: Each antibody has a shape that is complementary to the antigen on the measles virus.
steps.decision: Name the shape word the marks want, complementary, and what it matches: the antigen, not the whole virus.

steps.working: The chickenpox virus carries antigens of a different shape, so the antibody does not fit them.
steps.decision: Then compare: a different antigen shape means no fit, so no attachment.

prompt: How does the shape of an antibody compare with the shape of the antigen it attaches to?
options: it is complementary to the antigen
it is the same shape as the antigen
answer: it is complementary to the antigen
explain: This is step 1 of the See it. The antibody's tip is the reverse of the antigen, a socket its point slides into, not a copy of it. And it fits the antigen on the surface, not the whole microorganism. The word is complementary.

optionNotes.option: it is the same shape as the antigen
optionNotes.why: It sounds right because the two fit, but a copy of the antigen's shape could not slide over it: the antibody is its reverse.
The antibody fits one small molecule on the surface, the antigen, not the outline of the whole microorganism.

twin.prompt: An antibody attaches to a bacterium. Which part of the bacterium does its shape fit?
twin.explain: Antibodies are made against antigens, the molecules on a microorganism's surface, and fit those alone: complementary to the antigen, not to the whole cell.

md: An antibody has more than one tip, so it can hold two microorganisms at once. Thousands do this and **clump** them together. Stuck in a clump, they cannot spread or reproduce, so there are fewer to cause symptoms. A different white blood cell, a **phagocyte**, then **engulfs** the clump and **digests** it.

title: Three words, three marks
md: The Summer 2024 report wanted the standard terms here: name the phagocyte, say it engulfs, say it digests. 'The white blood cells eat them' names none of the three.

stem: A splinter carries bacteria into a finger, and antibodies attach to them. Describe how the bacteria are then destroyed. [4]

steps.working: The antibodies clump the bacteria together.
steps.decision: Start where the stem leaves off: attached antibodies hold the bacteria in clumps.

steps.working: Clumped bacteria cannot spread or reproduce.
steps.decision: Say what clumping achieves before anything destroys them.

steps.working: A phagocyte engulfs a clump, surrounding it.
steps.decision: Name the cell and the verb: phagocyte, engulfs.

steps.working: The phagocyte digests the bacteria inside it.
steps.decision: The last word the marks want: digests.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Immune System"
why: Phagocytes, lymphocytes and antibodies, made for another exam board: it adds antitoxins, which CCEA does not examine, and leaves out active and passive immunity, which it does.

prompt: After antibodies clump microorganisms together, a phagocyte engulfs the clump and then ______ it.
answer: digests | digest | digested | breaks down | break down | breaks it down | digests it | digest it | breaks them down | digests them | digesting
explain: This is step 4 of the See it. A phagocyte deals with a clump in two steps: first it engulfs it, surrounding it, then it digests the microorganisms inside. The step asked for is the second: it digests it.

twin.prompt: Before a phagocyte can digest a clump of microorganisms, it first ______ the clump.
twin.answer: engulfs | engulf | engulfs it | surrounds | surround | surrounds it | takes it in | ingests | wraps around it
twin.explain: The phagocyte's two steps come in order: it engulfs the clump, surrounding it, and only then digests what is inside. The first step is engulfs.

text: 4. Two white blood cells, two jobs

md: Two kinds of white blood cell share the work, and the marks depend on keeping them apart. **Lymphocytes** make antibodies, each against one antigen. **Phagocytes** engulf and digest. Platelets are not white blood cells at all: they start clotting.

stem: A blood test counts two kinds of white blood cell. State what each kind does when bacteria get into the body. [2]

steps.working: Lymphocytes make antibodies against the bacteria's antigens.
steps.decision: One cell, one job: say which chemical lymphocytes make.

steps.working: Phagocytes engulf the bacteria and digest them.
steps.decision: The other cell, the other job: the two verbs of phagocytosis.

prompt: Which white blood cells make antibodies?
explain: This is step 1 of the See it. Lymphocytes make antibodies against a particular antigen; phagocytes engulf and digest; platelets are not white blood cells and start clotting. Antibodies come from lymphocytes.

optionNotes.why: Phagocytes are white blood cells too, which makes them tempting, but their job is to engulf and digest: they make no antibodies.
Platelets are in the blood and help defend the body by starting a clot, but they are not white blood cells and make no antibodies.

twin.prompt: Which white blood cells engulf and digest microorganisms?
twin.explain: Step 2 of the See it: phagocytes engulf and digest. Lymphocytes make antibodies instead, and platelets start clotting.

alt: A graph of antibody concentration against time. After the first exposure, on day 0, antibodies appear on day 5 and rise slowly to a small peak of 25 units on day 12. After a second exposure to the same antigen, on day 35, antibodies appear on day 37 and rise fast to a peak of 75 units on day 41.
caption: After the second exposure to the same antigen, antibodies appear sooner and reach a far higher level.

md: The first time a microorganism gets in, making the right antibodies takes days, and you may feel ill meanwhile. Some of the lymphocytes then stay in the blood as **memory lymphocytes**. If the same microorganism returns, they recognise its antigen at once, and antibodies are made faster, in greater numbers, and last longer.

stem: The graph shows one person's antibody concentration after two exposures to the same microorganism. Compare the two responses.

steps.working: First exposure: antibodies appear after 5 days and peak at 25 units.
steps.decision: Read the first hump: when the line leaves the axis, then its top against the grid.

steps.working: Second exposure, on day 35: antibodies appear after 2 days and peak at 75 units.
steps.decision: Count the days from the second exposure, day 35, not from day 0.

steps.working: 75 ÷ 25 = 3: the second response is faster, 3 times larger, and lasts longer.
steps.decision: How many times greater means divide the larger peak by the smaller, never subtract.

prompt: On another person's antibody graph, the first peak is 15 units and the peak after a second exposure to the same antigen is 75 units. How many times greater is the second peak?
explain: This is step 3 of the See it. "How many times greater" asks for a division, the larger peak over the smaller, not a subtraction: 75 ÷ 15 = 5 times greater.

twin.prompt: A first antibody peak is 18 units, and the peak after a second exposure to the same antigen is 72 units. How many times greater is the second peak?
twin.explain: Divide the larger peak by the smaller: 72 ÷ 18 = 4 times greater. Subtracting would give how many units higher, which is not what is asked.

md: Ask one question: did your own lymphocytes make the antibodies? If yes, after an infection or a vaccine, it is **active immunity**, and it lasts because memory lymphocytes remain. If the antibodies arrived ready-made, across the placenta before birth, in a mother's milk or by injection, it is **passive immunity**.

Passive immunity works at once but fades: the antibodies are broken down, nothing replaces them, and no memory lymphocytes were made. A graph shows it as a falling line against the level needed for immunity.

stem: A patient is injected with antibodies on day 0 at 96 units. The graph shows the level falling; 24 units are needed for immunity. For how long is the patient immune, and why does it end?

steps.working: Immune from day 0: the level starts at 96 units, above the 24 needed.
steps.decision: Ready-made antibodies protect at once: no days of waiting as there are when lymphocytes must make them.

steps.working: The curve crosses the dashed line at 24 units on day 16, the last day of immunity.
steps.decision: Read along the level needed to where the curve meets it, then down to the days.

steps.working: It ends because the injected antibodies are broken down and no memory lymphocytes were made: passive immunity.
steps.decision: Name the type from who made the antibodies: not her lymphocytes, so passive.

prompt: A newborn baby gets antibodies from its mother's milk. What type of immunity is this?
explain: This is step 3 of the See it. The deciding question is who made the antibodies: not the baby's lymphocytes, since they arrived ready-made in the milk. Ready-made antibodies give passive immunity, quick but short-lived.

optionNotes.why: The baby is protected, which feels active, but its own lymphocytes made nothing: the antibodies came ready-made in the milk, so it is passive.
The antibodies in the milk do protect the baby, for a while; protection from ready-made antibodies is passive immunity.

twin.prompt: A child is vaccinated and her own lymphocytes make antibodies. What type of immunity is this?
twin.explain: Her own lymphocytes made the antibodies, so it is active immunity, and it lasts because memory lymphocytes remain.

md: **Choose the antibody** (2023). Look for the socket the antigen would slot into. A has tips the same shape as the antigen, so no; C has a square socket, so no; B has a triangular socket, the reverse of the triangular antigen. Answer: B, because its shape is complementary.

**Read the level needed** (2021): a line on the graph marks the level needed for immunity, so read the first and last days the curve is above it. **Why no symptoms the second time?** (2025): the marks go to memory lymphocytes and what they do, not to antibodies being specific.

stem: Marking two answers to 'Explain why a person infected a second time by the same bacterium has no symptoms. [3]'. X: 'The antibodies are specific to that bacterium.' Y: 'Memory lymphocytes recognise it, so antibodies are made faster and in greater numbers.'

steps.working: X: 0 marks. Every antibody is specific, the first time too, so it explains nothing new.
steps.decision: Ask of each line: what is different the second time? The 2025 report found this answer often.

steps.working: Y: memory lymphocytes recognise the bacterium.
steps.decision: The difference is in the blood: cells kept from the first infection.

steps.working: Y: antibodies are made faster, and in greater numbers.
steps.decision: Two more points: how soon and how many, so the bacteria are destroyed before symptoms.

prompt: A question asks why a person infected a second time with the same bacterium has no symptoms. Which answer earns the marks?
options: memory lymphocytes make antibodies faster and in greater numbers
the antibodies are specific to that bacterium
the bacterium is weaker the second time
answer: memory lymphocytes make antibodies faster and in greater numbers
explain: This is answer Y in the See it. The question is about what is different the second time: being specific is true the first time too, and the bacterium is the same. The memory lymphocytes are new, so antibodies come faster and in greater numbers.

optionNotes.option: the antibodies are specific to that bacterium
optionNotes.why: True of every antibody, the first time as well, so it explains nothing new; the 2025 report found this answer often.

optionNotes.option: the bacterium is weaker the second time
optionNotes.why: The bacterium is the same both times; what has changed is the blood, which now holds memory lymphocytes.

twin.prompt: A student explains why a vaccinated person does not fall ill when infected. Which line earns a mark?
options: memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen at once
antibodies are specific to one antigen
twin.answer: memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen at once
twin.explain: The vaccine left memory lymphocytes, which is what differs when the real microorganism arrives. Being specific is true of all antibodies, and a vaccine does not kill the microorganism.

Name the barriers, **skin**, **mucous membranes** and **blood clotting**, and describe how a clot forms.
Explain that **lymphocytes** make **antibodies** complementary to one **antigen**.
Describe clumping, then a **phagocyte** that engulfs and digests.
Explain the faster, larger second response with **memory lymphocytes**, and tell **active** from **passive** immunity.

Expect a short question on both tiers: barriers to name, an antibody to choose or explain, what happens after clumping, or why the second response is different. The marks are nearly all words: complementary, antigen, phagocyte, engulf, digest, memory lymphocytes. Stuck? Write the steps in order, one short sentence each.
